results.result: The study employed a viral vector-based approach to create a macaque model of Huntington's disease by administering a 1:1 mixture of AAV2-HTT85Q and AAV2.retro-HTT85Q (Group 85Q, n=6) or control vectors (Group 10Q, n=6; Group Buffer, n=5) into the caudate and putamen of 17 adult rhesus macaques. Animals underwent longitudinal behavioral testing and multimodal neuroimaging over 30 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 and C183-C185 provide clear methodological details including group assignments, vector compositions, injection sites, sample sizes, and ethical approvals. The experimental design is well-documented with appropriate controls (both 10Q and buffer groups), and the study received proper institutional approval (C184-C185).

results.result: 85Q-treated macaques exhibited significant spatial working memory deficits on the 3-Choice Spatial Delayed Response (SDR) task compared to both control groups, with deficits emerging at 3 months and persisting through 30 months post-surgery. A three-way ANOVA revealed significant main effects of group (p=0.0004) and timepoint (p=0.019), with 85Q animals performing significantly worse than Buffer (p=0.00014) and 10Q (p=0.0028) controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C48 provide comprehensive statistical evidence for working memory deficits in 85Q animals. The ANOVA results (C41) are appropriately reported with F-statistics and p-values, post-hoc comparisons are clearly stated (C42-C43), and the temporal progression is well-documented (C44-C45). The finding that both control groups improved over time (C48) while 85Q animals did not strengthens the interpretation of disease-related cognitive decline.

results.result: 85Q-treated animals demonstrated impaired fine motor skill performance on the Lifesaver Retrieval Task, showing significantly reduced practice effects and increased retrieval latencies compared to controls. A three-way ANOVA revealed significant main effects of Group (p=0.006) and Timepoint (p=3.121E-10), with 85Q animals performing significantly worse than Buffer (p=0.002) and 10Q (p=0.049) controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C61 provide robust statistical evidence for motor skill deficits. The ANOVA results (C53) show highly significant effects, and the finding that Buffer controls improved while 85Q animals showed reduced practice effects or increased latencies (C55-C56) demonstrates disease-related motor impairment. The temporal analysis (C59-C61) shows consistent group differences across multiple timepoints.

results.result: 85Q-treated macaques developed progressive motor phenotypes beginning at 2-3 months post-surgery, including orofacial dyskinesia, forelimb postural changes, chorea, bradykinesia, and tremor, which persisted through 30 months. A two-way ANOVA of neurological rating scale (NRS) scores revealed significant effects of Group (p<0.0001), Timepoint (p<0.0001), and their interaction (p<0.0001), with 85Q animals showing significantly higher NRS scores than both control groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C75 provide detailed observational and statistical evidence for motor phenotypes. The NRS was administered by blinded raters (C64), strengthening the validity of the findings. The ANOVA results (C65) show highly significant effects, and the descriptive observations (C71-C74) provide specific phenotypic details that align with HD symptomatology. The temporal progression from early orofacial symptoms to later bradykinesia and tremor (C71-C74) mirrors human disease progression.

results.result: Motor phenotypes in 85Q-treated animals were significantly exacerbated by the dopamine agonist apomorphine (0.3 mg/kg), with a three-way ANOVA revealing significant main effects of Group (p<0.0001), Timepoint (p<0.0001), and ApoCondition (p<0.0001), as well as significant interactions. 85Q animals showed significantly elevated NRS scores post-apomorphine at 3, 6, 9, and 20 months, while control groups showed no significant changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C84 provide strong evidence for dopaminergic modulation of motor phenotypes, which is clinically relevant to HD. The experimental design (C79) is appropriate, the statistical analysis (C81-C82) is comprehensive with significant main effects and interactions, and the selective effect in 85Q animals (C83-C84) demonstrates disease-specific dopaminergic dysfunction. This finding aligns with known HD pathophysiology (C76-C78).

results.result: 85Q-treated macaques exhibited significant white matter microstructural changes as measured by DTI, with reductions in fractional anisotropy (FA) appearing as early as 3 months post-surgery and persisting through 30 months. Changes showed an anterior-posterior gradient with largest reductions in prefrontal WM tracts, corona radiata, internal/external capsules, and corpus callosum. A repeated measures ANOVA revealed significant main effects of Group (p<0.0001) and Timepoint (p=0.003), and FA decreases correlated significantly with all three behavioral measures (NRS: r=-0.920, p<0.001; Lifesaver: r=-0.746, p<0.001; SDR: r=0.806, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C96 provide comprehensive evidence for white matter pathology with appropriate statistical analyses and strong correlations with behavior. The DTI methodology is standard (C86), the spatial distribution of changes (C89-C90) is well-characterized, and the statistical analysis (C91-C93) shows highly significant group effects. The strong correlations between FA changes and all three behavioral measures (C94-C96) provide convergent validity for the imaging findings as disease biomarkers.

results.result: Additional DTI analyses revealed that 85Q animals showed significant elevations in radial diffusivity (RD) and mean diffusivity (MD), as well as decreases in axial diffusivity (AD) compared to controls (all p<0.01). RD and MD increases generally overlapped with FA decreases in prefrontal WM tracts, corona radiata, internal/external capsules, and corpus callosum, while AD decreases were more widely distributed. No changes in these parameters survived thresholding in control groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C104 provide complementary DTI metrics that strengthen the interpretation of white matter pathology. The consistent findings across multiple DTI parameters (FA, RD, MD, AD) with similar spatial distributions (C100-C102) provide convergent evidence for white matter degeneration. The observation that AD decreases were more widely distributed (C103) suggests both demyelination and axonal damage, consistent with HD pathology.

results.result: Tensor-based morphometry (TBM) revealed significant tissue atrophy in 85Q animals beginning at 3 months post-surgery and persisting through 30 months, primarily affecting the caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, and frontal/motor cortical areas. A two-way repeated measures ANOVA showed significant main effects of Group (p<0.001) and Timepoint (p<0.001), with 85Q animals showing significantly greater tissue contractions than both control groups. TBM changes correlated significantly with all three behavioral measures (NRS: r=0.786, p<0.001; Lifesaver: r=0.730, p<0.001; SDR: r=-0.683, p=0.002).
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C115 provide robust evidence for regional brain atrophy using appropriate methodology. The TBM approach is well-established for detecting structural changes (C105-C106), the statistical analysis (C111-C112) shows highly significant group effects, and the spatial distribution of atrophy (C110) matches regions known to be affected in HD. The strong correlations with behavioral measures (C113-C115) demonstrate clinical relevance of the structural changes.

results.result: Resting-state fMRI analysis identified four independent components (ICs), with IC2 (involving striatal and sensory-motor areas) showing the most protracted changes. 85Q animals exhibited significant decreases in IC2 connectivity beginning at 3 months and continuing through 30 months, particularly in VLPFC, VMPFC, SSC, putamen, substantia nigra, globus pallidus, amygdala, and hippocampus. A two-way repeated measures ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of Group (p<0.0001), and IC2 connectivity decreases correlated significantly with all three behavioral measures (NRS: r=-0.924, p<0.001; Lifesaver: r=-0.672, p=0.003; SDR: r=0.857, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C130 provide strong evidence for functional connectivity disruption using appropriate ICA methodology. The identification of four ICs (C117-C121) is data-driven and unbiased, the focus on IC2 (C122) is justified by its involvement of striatal-motor circuits relevant to HD, and the statistical analysis (C126-C127) shows highly significant group effects. The very strong correlations with behavioral measures (C128-C130) demonstrate that functional connectivity changes are clinically meaningful biomarkers.

results.result: Additional resting-state network changes were observed in 85Q animals, including late-emerging decreases in IC3 connectivity at 30 months (affecting prefrontal cortex, caudate, and medial thalamus), transient increases in IC1 connectivity that returned to baseline by 6 months, and subtle changes in IC4. No changes in IC1, IC3, or IC4 survived thresholding in control groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C136 describe additional functional connectivity changes that provide a more complete picture of network disruption. The late emergence of IC3 changes (C131-C132) suggests progressive network involvement, while the transient IC1 changes (C134) may reflect early compensatory mechanisms. The absence of significant changes in control groups (C136) strengthens the interpretation that these are disease-specific effects.

results.result: Histological evaluation at 30 months post-surgery revealed widespread em48+ mHTT aggregates in 85Q animals but not controls, with aggregates found throughout the caudate and putamen (injection sites) and in deeper cortical layers (V/VI) of multiple cortical regions including prefrontal, premotor, supplemental motor, anterior cingulate, primary motor, and insular cortices, as well as subcortical regions (amygdala, thalamus, globus pallidus, claustrum, hippocampus, substantia nigra). Triple-label immunofluorescence confirmed that aggregates were located in neurons but not astrocytes, primarily in the nucleus, with some extracellular foci in neuropil and localized areas of white matter tracts.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C146 provide comprehensive histological validation of mHTT expression and aggregate formation. The use of em48 antibody is appropriate for detecting polyQ-expanded HTT (C138), the spatial distribution matches the expected pattern based on viral vector delivery and retrograde transport (C139-C142), and the cellular localization studies (C143-C145) provide important mechanistic insights. The presence of aggregates in white matter tracts (C146) is explained by viral vector dispersion during injection (C167).

results.result: The HTT85Q macaque model recapitulates key features of early-stage human HD, including motor and cognitive deficits accompanied by microstructural alterations, atrophy, and reduced functional connectivity throughout the cortico-basal ganglia network. The reduction in WM FA closely mirrors changes in human HD patients, and the overall patterns of neurodegeneration model changes detected in prodromal and early-stage HD patients. Histological evaluation confirmed mHTT expression and aggregate formation in the same brain regions affected at 10 weeks post-surgery, suggesting stable aggregation without additional regional involvement over time.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C158 provide a comprehensive summary of the model's validity and translational relevance. The comparison to human HD (C148, C150) is supported by appropriate citations, the behavioral and imaging findings are well-integrated (C147), and the histological validation (C156-C158) confirms the molecular basis of the observed phenotypes. The stability of aggregate distribution over time (C158) is an important finding for understanding disease progression in this model.

results.result: The spatial distribution of em48+ mHTT aggregates in 85Q animals showed an anterior-to-posterior gradient (highest in prefrontal/premotor cortices, moderate in motor/somatosensory cortices, less in temporal/parietal cortices, minimal in occipital cortices) that matches the pattern seen in human HD cases. Aggregates were predominantly in deeper cortical layers (V/VI), which serve as primary output layers to subcortical structures. Robust em48+ aggregates were confirmed in brain regions showing the most significant TBM atrophy and DTI changes, with aggregates in white matter largely located in and around needle tracts due to viral vector dispersion during injection.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C167 provide detailed spatial characterization of mHTT pathology with strong translational relevance. The anterior-posterior gradient (C160-C161) and laminar distribution (C162-C163) match human HD patterns, supported by appropriate citations (C159, C161, C163). The correspondence between histological findings and imaging changes (C164-C165) provides important validation of the imaging biomarkers. The explanation for white matter aggregates (C166-C167) is reasonable given the injection methodology.

results.result: The behavioral and imaging findings in HTT85Q macaques correlated strongly with each other, constituting a comprehensive set of outcome measures for future therapeutic evaluations. Viral-mediated HD macaques offer advantages over transgenic models, including the ability to generate larger cohorts and flexibility in model design (different promoters, HTT fragment lengths, CAG repeat lengths, capsid serotypes) in a shorter timeframe and with less expense compared to transgenic models.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C172 provide a balanced assessment of the model's utility and advantages. The strong correlations between behavioral and imaging measures (C168) are well-documented throughout the results. The comparison to transgenic models (C169-C171) is supported by appropriate citations (C170-C171), and the advantages of viral-vector approaches (C172) are reasonable given the flexibility in experimental design.

results.result: Future optimization of the AAV-based macaque model may be achievable by expanding the HTT fragment length, lowering the CAG repeat number (given the correlation between CAG length and age at disease onset in HD patients), or manipulating the CAA/CAG cassette (which associates with disease progression scores in human HD patients) to hasten or prolong disease progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C176 are speculative suggestions for future model optimization (C173, C176 explicitly marked as speculation). While the suggestions are reasonable and supported by citations to relevant human HD studies (C174-C175), they represent untested hypotheses rather than demonstrated results. These claims should be considered as discussion points for future work rather than supported findings.

results.result: The AAV2:2retro-HTT85Q model has several acknowledged limitations, including: (1) expression of only the N171 N-terminal fragment of mHTT due to viral vector packaging constraints, (2) potential intermediate behavioral effects in the 10Q control group due to expression of a truncated wildtype HTT fragment, (3) use of a strong CAG promoter rather than an endogenous HTT promoter, (4) presence of two wildtype endogenous HTT alleles in addition to the pathogenic transgene, (5) lack of introns precluding formation of alternatively spliced variants, and (6) limited expression to areas of transduction rather than ubiquitous brain and peripheral expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C177-C182 provide an honest and comprehensive assessment of model limitations. The packaging constraint (C177) is a well-known limitation of AAV vectors, the speculation about 10Q intermediate effects (C178) is reasonable given the observed behavioral differences between 10Q and Buffer groups (C47, C61, C70), and the other limitations (C179-C181) are clearly stated. The acknowledgment that the current model achieved broader expression than previous models but not ubiquitous expression (C182) provides appropriate context.

results.result: The introduction provides background on Huntington's disease (HD) as a genetic neurodegenerative disorder caused by expanded CAG/CAA repeats in the HTT gene, characterized by widespread cortico-basal ganglia pathology including striatal atrophy, white matter degeneration, mHTT aggregate formation, neuronal death, and gliosis. HD patients suffer from progressive motor dysfunction (chorea, bradykinesia, dystonia, rigidity), cognitive decline (working memory impairment, executive dysfunction), and psychiatric symptoms (depression, anxiety, irritability), with no current treatments capable of slowing disease progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C12 provide well-established background information about HD, all supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for developing improved animal models of HD.

results.result: The introduction reviews existing HD animal models, noting that while rodent models have advanced understanding of HD pathophysiology, they do not fully recapitulate human behavioral symptoms, and species differences limit translational potential. None of the therapies showing efficacy in mouse models have succeeded in clinical trials. Large animal models (sheep, minipigs, NHPs) have emerged as critical tools, with viral-mediated NHP models offering advantages. Recent AAV capsid variants with enhanced retrograde/anterograde transport properties enable transduction of entire neural circuits, and previous work demonstrated that AAV2.retro-mHTT85Q delivery to macaque striatum results in mHTT expression and aggregate formation throughout cortical and subcortical striatal afferents.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C33 provide comprehensive background on animal models and the rationale for the current study, all supported by appropriate citations. The review of rodent model limitations (C14-C19) and the description of viral vector advances (C30-C33) establish the scientific foundation for the experimental approach.

results.result: The manuscript provides relevant background on HD clinical features and biomarkers, including: (1) cognitive decline (working memory impairment) sometimes preceding motor dysfunction, (2) motor task performance abnormalities emerging in prodromal HD individuals <5 years from diagnosis, (3) motor phenotypes being modulated by dopamine with FDA-approved VMAT2 inhibitors used to treat chorea, (4) reduced FA in multiple WM regions indicating microstructural changes, (5) brain atrophy detected by TBM in symptomatic HD with some changes beginning prior to symptom onset, (6) decreased RSFC in premanifest HD-gene carriers shifting to increased RSFC in later stages, and (7) progressive loss of striatal dopamine receptor density correlating with clinical severity.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C159 (selected) provide relevant clinical and imaging background information, all supported by appropriate citations to the HD literature. These claims establish the clinical relevance of the behavioral and imaging measures used in the study.
